Definition: from ἄγαν (much) and ἄχθος (grief; akin to the base of G43); to be greatly afflicted, i.e. (figuratively) indignant:--be much (sore) displeased, have (be moved with, with) indignation.
BiblicalUsage: Aganakteo is to be greatly displeased, moved with indignation. The ten disciples were moved with indignation against James and John; the disciples were indignant when the ointment was poured out; Jesus was much displeased when they kept the children away; and the ruler of the synagogue was indignant because Jesus healed on the Sabbath. The word covers indignation that is petty, indignation that is wasteful, indignation that is righteous, and indignation that is blind — and the story always shows which is which.
TheologicalSignificance: What this word teaches me is that anger is not one thing. The disciples' indignation was envy, the ruler's was religion without mercy, and Jesus' was love defending little children — and I hold that the difference is everything, because God weighs the heart behind the heat.
